title: Union with Christ
aliases: union with christ in biblical theology
summary: These passages use several images to describe shared life with Christ. John 15 compares disciples to branches that depend on the vine and bear fruit. Romans 6 connects baptism with Christ’s death and resurrection, then calls believers to live differently. Galatians 2 says Christ lives in Paul; Ephesians 2 describes believers as made alive and raised with Christ; Colossians 3 speaks of their life as hidden with Christ and directs them toward new conduct. The images express relationship and participation but are not identical metaphors.
historical_context: The references include Jesus’ teaching in John and letters addressed to Christian communities. Their textual settings support an account of how the writings describe life with Christ; the sources do not establish additional social or historical reconstruction.
canonical_context: John uses the vine and branches to describe dependence and fruitfulness. Paul’s letters use participation language: dying and rising with Christ, Christ living in the believer, being made alive with Christ, and a life hidden with Christ. These related descriptions connect identity and conduct while retaining the distinct argument in each passage.
literary_context: John 15 is a metaphor in Jesus’ teaching; Romans 6 reasons from baptism; Galatians 2 gives a personal confession; Ephesians 2 contrasts death and life; Colossians 3 draws ethical instruction from the believer’s life with Christ. The shift from image and confession to exhortation shows how the texts connect relationship with conduct.
covenantal_significance: The passages portray belonging to Christ as a source of new life and a changed way of living. Romans connects participation in Christ’s death and resurrection with refusing sin’s rule; Colossians connects life hidden with Christ to putting away harmful conduct. The relationship is presented as both gift and calling.
canonical_role: This entry gathers biblical images and arguments about shared life with Christ. It helps readers see how vine, death and resurrection, indwelling, and new life each illuminate relationship with Christ and its ethical consequences.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Union with Christ in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
